utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the outset, before we call our first proposed witness for the day, we, on the 29th of April, provided a letter for distribution to all parties, indicating the next 28 witnesses that we proposed to call. I might say that the first two, Mr. Isufi and Mr. Kabashi, are 92 bis witness proposals for whom we already have permission by the Trial Chamber to call as 92 bis. There then follow a number of witnesses, numbers 3 through 18 on our list, but for two of them which will not require that ruling now, that we have not yet received ruling to proceed, and I anticipate at the rate at which we hope to go, we will actually get to some of those witnesses who are here today and ready to start testifying. And just alerting the Court that we're going to require a ruling before we can actually call those witnesses. Also, over the weekend, a review reveals that number 3 on our list, Shaqiri, there appears to be a problem in that the witness gave two statements, only one of which has been bis'ed. So until that matter is resolved, we'll go -- we'll skip number 3 so that we can resolve that technical issue and go number 1, 2, 4, 5. So first will be Isufi, then Mr. Kabashi, then we'll skip Shaqiri, and in the event the Court permits 92 bis for Haradinaj and Gerxhaliu, that should probably do for today. I just thought I'd give you that indication that we've got some rulings to obtain before we can proceed, after the first two witnesses. With that preliminary matter, I would propose to call Perparim Isufi as our first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Isufi, I understand, sir, that you are 22 years old and you are at this moment unmarried. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone on, please. We can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently it will take a few minutes to sort out the problem. We shall wait. Mr. Ryneveld, I don't think there's anything we can usefully do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. The only thing I might indicate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ryneveld, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. The only thing I might suggest is if the Court wants to find the location of the next village on the map while we're waiting. Anything to save a few minutes. Exhibit 83, page 6, on the right-hand column, you'll see number 14, and about an inch to the left of that number 14, you'll see an orange sort of marking with Mazgit, and that, I understand, will be the community that this witness will be talking about. Other than that, I think I should wait until we have the go-ahead to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, can -- oh, you'll have to put the headphones on. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Isufi, do I understand correctly that you are a 22-year-old, unmarried Muslim of ethnic -- Albanian ethnicity, living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you live in the village of Mazgit, in the municipality of Obilic, in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what was your occupation at the time? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I used to go to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, did you give a statement to officials from the ICTY on the 10th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently, did someone read -- or give you a copy in Albanian of that statement on the 2nd of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read over that statement and agree that that was -- that the contents of that statement were true and accurate to the best of your belief?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at that time, you swore a solemn declaration before a presiding officer of this Court, indicating that it was true to the best of your knowledge and belief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that statement now be tendered as an exhibit in these proceedings, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 117.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 117, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see the registry?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. If it please the Court, I propose to read a very brief summary of what is contained in the statement. Your Honours, according to the statement, on the morning of the 27th of March, 1999, the witness and his family were forced to flee their home, and half of the women and children fled the village and went to Pristina, due to the mobilisation of the Serb forces around this village. That afternoon, the Serbs started to shell the village of Mazgit. The remaining villagers fled to the village of Bariljevo. The witness spent the night in Bariljevo before returning to his village. At noon the following day, the witness could hear automatic gunfire and shells falling, and he therefore fled and headed for Pristina, with the remaining women and children. En route to Pristina, a vehicle containing three men dressed in blue camouflage police uniforms pulled up. They appeared to be heavily armed with automatic weapons, and they opened fire on the group, killing four of the women. The balance of the group ran the rest of the way to Pristina. In his statement, this witness describes the incidents en route in some detail. The witness describes in his statement that a few days later, he heard from a passerby that the police were forcibly expelling people and that a number of Albanian people were being killed. The witness and his family left and were then directed by police to walk around the city with many others. The column, which, in his estimate, by that time numbered in the thousands, were eventually directed by police to the Dragodan train station in Pristina, where they were ordered to get on an overcrowded train. They had no idea where they were going and were not allowed to get off the train. The witness saw many Serb police and army. He noted that the Serbs set fire to two houses on each side of the train. He then describes more about what happened and indicates that they arrived near the border early the next morning, when the people on the train were told to disembark and walk up the tracks to the Macedonian border. That is a very brief summary of the witness's statement, but Your Honours have the full statement tendered as Exhibit 117. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did they, as you say - the Serbs - start shelling your village on the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to say; it's for those who were doing the shelling. Did you see any reason for shelling of your village that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes; only because we were Albanians. That's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what time did this happen?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: It was about 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many inhabitants, on that occasion in your village, were killed?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: You think on the 27th of March, when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No one was killed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago you said that they shelled the village to kill the Albanians, but nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: They shelled the village, but one hour before they did that, the children and the men left, and only young men and a few young -- a few men, adults, remained in the village. And we too left to Bariljeve after the shelling started, and that day, I repeat, no one was hurt or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the soldiers shelled an empty village in which there were just a few people and that they did not know that the village was empty, in fact; is that it?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I don't know if they knew that the village was empty, but they started shelling at around 3.00, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did the police in February of that same year, close to your village, as you say, at 800 metres, set up a checkpoint? Do you know anything about that? Do you know the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, I don't know the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did, as you say, the Serbs, up until 1999, or rather, those developments which you're describing now, maltreat anybody from your village, or kill anybody?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. Until that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, do you say in your statement that your relatives and you were afraid that the Serbs would first abuse you and then kill you?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I said because we were afraid, since we saw that the situation was deteriorating with every passing day, and we saw checkpoints set up in close vicinity to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you see any members of the KLA in the vicinity of the village?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. There wasn't any, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you see the KLA for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: It was very late that I saw them. In fact, I saw them only on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you see them first off television, live?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: In March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you see them on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: In Llap area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that? I mean, you said it was March, but when in March?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly, in relation to what you were saying about the 27th of March. So you saw them before the 27th of March. How many days before?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: About ten days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So ten days before -- you saw members of the KLA ten days before the village was shelled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: There were only two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons were they carrying?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I don't know. I never looked at them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they far away from you?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I saw -- I told you that I saw them only on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the two you say you saw some ten days before the village was shelled.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes. That was how it was, ten days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you. How far away were they from you when you weren't able to see what weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I saw them only on television, I said. I didn't see them armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said that you saw two in the Lap area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question that you were asked is: When did you first see any KLA off television, live? And you said: In March 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was on television. I never saw them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is quite clear. Let's go on. When did you hear of the KLA? When did you first learn about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: It was rather late when I first heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, "late"? When? Approximately when?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: At that time, March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that over television too?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you say in your statement as soon as you saw the Serb policemen, you started getting ready to flee from the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But before that, you said that the policemen had a checkpoint for quite a long time in your neighbourhood. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you were afraid of the police, why didn't you run away when you saw that they had a checkpoint there?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Because we just didn't think that they would go on to commit these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you ran away from the village, nothing had happened yet. How did you know, then, that somebody would commit some crimes, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: We knew because we just knew that, from day to day, they started to kill the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you: How come you knew? And your answer is: We knew because we knew. Can you tell me: How did you know, when nothing had happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think he's given the best answer he can. And we know that the shelling did in fact start. So it's not really going to take us much further to argue about why they left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what you said just now, "We know that the shelling did in fact start," that is very questionable. We can only say that the witness has been asserting that the shelling had started, but we do not know that it started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's his evidence, that the shelling started. You asked him: Why did you leave? And his answer was they knew trouble was coming. And in fact, according to him, trouble came. So there's not much point going on, little point going on, asking this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely why I'm putting this question: How did you know that they would shell the village? They were there for so long, so many days, and they didn't do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that they would start shelling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's any further point going on with this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't know, but -- we didn't know that they were going to shell until the moment when they started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not know that. And previously you said that you had known that it would happen. On that day, the 27th of March, in your village, apart from the local villagers, were there any other people there as well?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. Only us local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that half of the women and children left the village already in the early morning hours and went to Pristina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Because they were scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they scared of?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: They were scared of your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the forces had been there for months and weeks before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going round the same point. His evidence is that they were scared and they had something to be scared of and that shelling started. It's a waste of time to go on asking him why they were scared. He's told you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you with them on the way to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that only men stayed back in the village?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were the men armed?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bariljevo, at the village of Bariljevo, you claim that you walked into an empty house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Nothing. We only stayed there that night. We stayed there the night of 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you only spent the night there, was it all of you who had set out, these women, that is, and you together with them, you spent the night of the 27th of March there?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, those women were there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this house in Bariljevo, how far away is it from your village?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but about five or six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five or six kilometres? Well, you said that you had set out from the village at least an hour before the alleged shelling started, that the shelling started at 3.00, so you left at 2.00 at the latest. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as for the entire afternoon all way up to the evening, from 2.00 until the evening, you had passed only five kilometres?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who made you in charge of taking the women and children to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first question is: Was he in charge? Were you in charge of taking the women and children to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you were. Who was in charge of doing that?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: There was nobody in charge. We just set out that day for Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were the only man who went to Pristina together with the women and children, as part of that group?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all the rest remained in the village in order to take care of the cattle?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how many men stayed back in the village in order to take care of the safety of the cattle?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Eight or nine of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: How high was the embankment that you walked down when you left the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: You mean when we climbed up onto the embankment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's clear, Mr. Milosevic, we are now on the next day. Is this right, Mr. Isufi? You returned after the first shelling, you returned the following day to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But then, according to your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: According to your statement, there was then another shelling of the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the statement says the men in the village had decided -- "The men of the village had decided that if we were attacked again, I would be responsible for getting the remaining women and children to Pristina and that the men would stay within the village for as long as possible to make sure the cattle were safe." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So on that second day, you were responsible, were you, for getting the women and children to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. They left me to go with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then the shelling started. Were you in the village then, when the shelling started on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not then. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In any event, you and the women and children, a group of about 20, then set off towards Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We come to the time when you left the road and came down the embankment that the accused is asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this second time when you went to Pristina was actually on the next day?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, it was the next day, that Sunday, 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 27th, in the afternoon, you went to Pristina. That's what you said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. It was the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went to Pristina twice; the first time on the 27th, in the afternoon, and the second time on the 28th. This is in accordance with your statement and it's also in accordance with what you've just been saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not fair to the witness. He said on the first occasion they went to Bariljevo and that's where they spent the night. Then they came back to the village and the next day they set out for Pristina. That's what his statement says and that was his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the next day, somebody made you responsible of taking care of the women and children, taking them to Pristina. That's what you said only a short while ago.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I wasn't ordered to do this, but I took this upon myself, and we set off for Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a short while ago you said that you were responsible for taking the women and children to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I wasn't given a duty, but I was the only person left to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why were you the only person, when you say that there were seven or eight other men there as well, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Well, I was the youngest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that all the others had some more important business to attend to; right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't have important jobs to do. They were only sitting at home and looking at the situation and seeing what was going on, like on other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you went on the first day to Pristina and you covered only five kilometres, then how did you decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you musn't misrepresent the evidence. He didn't go to Pristina the first day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the intention was the first day to have the women and children go to Pristina; however, they didn't make it all the way to Pristina. Right? So that is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they decide to go back rather than continue their journey to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, we didn't decide to go back, but we went straight to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand you.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: We continued on the road straight to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Isufi, in your statement, page -- it is page 2, and third paragraph, at the end of the paragraph: "When I reached Bariljevo, I stayed in an empty house. This house had already been looted and the occupants were no longer there. The only members of my immediate family that were in Bariljevo was my brother, Arben, and myself." And you said: "All the other members of my family had fled to Pristina an hour or so before the shelling started." Did the other members of your family go to Pristina or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did, one hour before the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they different people from those who took care of the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some members of your family had fled to Pristina on 27th of March; is it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they not the same people as those who took -- who took with you to Pristina the next day? Are they different people or the same people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they were not the same people. They were different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be the confusion of the accused. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously there has been some confusion, but I'm not the one who caused it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not return to your village from Bariljevo; you continued your journey to Pristina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, on the 28th of March. It was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was it that returned to the village again? Was it only you or was it everybody together?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I said we didn't return to the village as of Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You left on the 27th of March, you spent the night in Bariljevo, and then you proceeded to Pristina. On the 28th of March, again you went from your village to Pristina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes. We left for Prishtina from our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the 27th and on the 28th of March, you were going to Pristina from your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to Prishtina on the 27th of March. I went to Bariljeve. I went to Prishtina on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you return from Bariljevo? You said that you spent the night in Bariljevo.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: We returned on the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Together?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these very same people that you went with to Bariljevo returned with you to the village and then the next day, again, you and these same people went to Pristina. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, you did. That was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a short while ago, in response to Mr. Kwon's question, you said that these were not the same people, and on the first day, it was one set of people that went and, the second day, it was a different set of people, and now you are claiming that it was the same people. What is correct: What you said a short while ago to Mr. Kwon or what you are saying to me now?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: The correct answer was the one I gave to Judge Kwon. On Saturday, my family and others left. But on Sunday, it was those women and men that we returned from Bariljeve to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then these same people went to Pristina again, together with you?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These same people who had left the previous day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have taken this as far as we can. Let us move on to another topic. You were talking about what happened on the journey to Pristina. It may be as well if we went on from there rather than going round and round on the same point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can move on because a major contradiction, discrepancy, is obvious here in these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this embankment that you've been describing. You said that this embankment constituted a major danger.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why was this embankment a major danger? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Because it was the main asphalt road, Prishtina-Mitrovica, near that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that on that road you didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No. When we went to -- on the way to Mitrovica, yes, but to Prishtina, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that, afterwards, a car appeared.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes. Once we crossed the main road, asphalt road, we went to that embankment, and then on the side road leaving to Obiliq, we saw that car approaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the vehicle was not driving along the road that you had already passed?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding from your statement that when you were watching the road, you didn't notice the vehicle, but then it got closer to you at a great speed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was the vehicle driving along the asphalt road or some other road?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: It was driving on the main, asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you said that the vehicle was not on the asphalt road, the main road, but that you saw a vehicle on a smaller byroad.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes. From that side road, then they turned and came to the road where they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this great speed that they were moving at, this was on the asphalt road. That is what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did they cross onto the side road and return to the main road? What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: They came and stopped when we crossed the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: When they came out of the car, it was night [as interpreted]. It was -- we were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: You mean when they came out of the car?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You were fleeing, you were afraid. How far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: We were very afraid, but they let us go on, on our way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Isufi, could you just concentrate on the question: How far away were the men, when they got out of the car, from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were very close to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of metres or something of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe 15 metres away, not further. Fifteen or twenty, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you -- in your statement, you explained how you crossed the road, that you didn't see them, and that afterwards, they appeared on the road. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we've been through this. Mr. Milosevic, this is the way the time is taken up, through repetition. He's explained. Now, we've got to the stage where the men were out of the car, they were 15 to 20 metres away from him. I suggest you move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you run as you were fleeing from them?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: We started to walk faster, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these people were wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did those masks look like?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: The usual masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean what you pull over your head; is that it?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With slits for the eyes and mouth, or no slits for the mouth?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could see them, if there were any slits, because I was very much scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that they had baseball caps.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when speaking of them, you said that they had baseball caps.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you know, I don't like to interfere. However, if the witness is going to be challenged by something he is alleged to have said in his statement, it ought to be accurate. I don't know whether it's a matter of translation in the copy that the witness -- that the accused is looking at, but in fairness, the witness does not have a statement in front of him, and there are a couple of points that are put to him now that he is alleged to have said that I can't find in the copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's get it straight. One is the baseball cap, which in the statement refers to a peaked-type cap. What was the other point?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There's a reference to masks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He agreed with the masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But it wasn't in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, but it was said -- it was said that it was -- that it was in the statement. These are the kinds of things that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it was. I mean, it was put, of course, in a misleading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us get the description from the witness now. Mr. Isufi --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we need to clear this up. What were these -- you tell us now: What were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what did they have on their heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were -- some of them had masks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did they have any sort of hats on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see them wearing any hats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you do anything more to describe the type of mask it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ones you put on your -- over your head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a question before I go on. You say some wore masks. How many of them wore masks?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I saw one of them wearing a mask. The others, I wasn't able to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about identifying them, but what did the others wear?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: The three of them had worn police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a moment ago, when asked by Mr. May, you said that they wore masks on their heads. I'm asking about their heads now.

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: I said masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that they didn't have anything else on their heads, in response to that same question; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, they didn't. No, they didn't have anything on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that I was wrong when I mentioned the baseball caps; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said they didn't have anything on, so there's no point going on with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me read you what I received from you. I didn't write this. It is a database of the International Crisis Group, and then all the rest of it is what the opposite side provided me with as being a witness statement with the facts, and it says, at the bottom, and it is page -- a page that has been marked 0305163. At the bottom of that page, there's a paragraph, which reads as follows: "I travelled with a group of 20 persons from Mazgit to Pristina. When we crossed the road at Orlovic, nearby a white Passat stopped, and it was moving at great speed. Three men got out of the car, wearing blue camouflage uniforms with black masks, baseball caps," and so on and so forth. Therefore -- have you found that passage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this statement, Mr. Milosevic? We haven't got it. We've got a reference to a peak-type cap.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was what was supplied with the statement from the International Crisis Group, and it was handed over together with the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, no doubt that's a separate statement which you disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Undoubtedly. We've disclosed everything regarding this witness, but this is not contained in the 92 bis material, but it's been disclosed to the accused, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what is put to you, Mr. Isufi, is this: That in a statement you made to the International Crisis Group, you describe the men as wearing blue camouflage uniforms with black masks and baseball caps. Can you -- in a moment, Mr. Tapuskovic. I'm asking the witness a question. Can you help us as to why you said that or whether there's an inaccuracy or something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say with caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement that Mr. Milosevic is referring to is under the number of 003163, and it has been disclosed. It was disclosed a long time ago. The amicus has it, and it is something which exists in the Prosecution documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I have a copy of that document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there's no mystery about this, you are under an obligation to disclose all the statements which you have which are relevant to what a witness has said. As far as the Court is concerned, you only serve on the Court, produce to the Court, the relevant documents which are to be admitted into evidence. This particular document is one which you've disclosed under your duty to do so; it has nothing to do with the document which you've disclosed to us. I'm just going to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you can disclose to us in due course -- I don't suppose you've got copies of that statement now, but we'll have it and we'll have it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was going to recommend that I do that. The document is clear. We can provide it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what we're going to do, Mr. Milosevic, is this: We're going to have this statement put into evidence. It will be an exhibit, this other statement. We've heard the discrepancy which you've referred to, and you can move on to the next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before I do so, one more question, please, as I don't know the procedure here. When you have two statements or several documents, now, if I point out a contradiction, do you enter it into evidence as an exhibit, or do you take separate decisions on when you're going to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It depends entirely on the circumstances. If a statement is exhibited, then of course it becomes part of the evidence and you will be able, in due course, to point out any discrepancies. If there are discrepancies of importance and the statement isn't before the Court, you can ask that it be put before the Court. That's your right, to ask that it be exhibited. So far in this case, I think I'm right in saying that if there have been important discrepancies, various statements have been exhibited during the course of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they're included whenever there has been a discrepancy of some kind. I merely wish to emphasise that every statement which speaks about incompatibility, or rather, the falsehood of the testimony, is relevant. But let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, therefore, a moment ago, that you were escaping, that it was night-time, and that you weren't able to see clearly or to notice the details. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: What date are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about that alleged appearance of the three men in a car. That's the event I'm referring to, the one you have been talking about. You say you were fleeing, it was night - that's what you said - and that you weren't able to see the details. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, this is not right. It was not at night. It was halfway through the day. It was about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand anything, then. A moment ago, the witness said that it was night-time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is right, but -- just a moment. It may be that there's a problem about the transcript, which we'll need to look into, or the translation. You see, Mr. Isufi --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself. It was he said, "I was afraid, I couldn't see." It was not night but it was misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. What time of day was it? Tell us again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about the masks and caps, you said that you were afraid, terrified, and that you couldn't say exactly -- you couldn't give us the details exactly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: That's right, except at that moment I just looked and then we started running.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as you were in that state, you were afraid and running and had your back turned to them, you said a moment ago that you couldn't give us the details, how then did you happen to notice this whole series of details that are written down in this paper that I quoted a moment ago? You said black masks, baseball caps, knives, rifles, bombs, all sorts of details which can be imagined on somebody's uniform. So you saw all those details, did you?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes, I saw these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I just have a few more questions. In your statement, the one you gave on the 10th of May, which was quoted at the beginning, you claim that you left Pristina, having decided to leave town after consulting with some people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is on page 6 of your statement, paragraph 2. Well, all right, let's not lose time. But you confirm that that is so, do you? Now, please answer my next question, which is linked to that, when you said that that was so. So after consulting some people about it, you decided to leave town. In the statement you gave to the members of the International Crisis Group, you state that you left Pristina because you were thrown out of your accommodation, your lodgings, when five members of the MUP ordered you to leave immediately. Now, tell me what is the correct version: What it says in your statement, which you have just confirmed, or this second thing that is contained in what you -- in the statement you made to the International Crisis Group? Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: The truth is that on Sunday we went, and on the 30th we -- the next day, we left Prishtina because they had started to expel the citizens of Prishtina and throw them out into the city streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you very specifically which of these two of your statements is correct. I'm not asking you about what you think about the population of Pristina, the citizens of Pristina, but you are testifying to what happened to you. And according to these two statements, what happened to you was two things: Either the first contained in the statement or the second in the statement of the International Crisis Group. Which is correct; the first or the second?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: What I said is exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Help us with this: Did members of the MUP order you to leave your accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They started to throw out groups of people out of Dragodan, out of the neighbourhood where we had been. They started to expel them in the direction of Prishtina city centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you just to confirm what you said in your statement of the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's difficult for a witness, particularly if he hasn't got the copy of the statement in front of him, to be able to answer a question like that. If he had the statement, yes, but he hasn't. Now, what he said is that he was told -- he was talking about leaving and he wasn't told to leave by members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't understand why, if the witness is telling the truth, he has to have a written statement, because the truth is one; it is a single truth. He is testifying about what happened to him. Why would he need a written statement to remember his testimony? He knows what happened to him, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, he has -- you are asking him: Which statement is right? You then read out a section of two statements. It is liable to confuse a witness when you then ask which of the statements is right. That is the point. He hasn't got a copy of it. Now, unless you've got something else about this particular point, we will move on. You must bring your cross-examination to a close by the break because you will have had much more than the usual time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will bring it to a close by the break. There's no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So regardless of the statements, a moment ago you confirmed - and I'm asking you again whether it is right that you decided to leave the town after having consulted some people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: No, that's not right. On the 30th, the police started to throw out the populous into the town of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you conscious of the fact that a moment ago, when I asked you whether it was right that you decided to leave town after consulting some people, your answer was: Yes, that is correct. Now you say: No, that is not correct. What is the truth: What you said five minutes ago or what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: What I say now is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, five minutes ago did you say that what -- in response to my question that that was correct if you say that what you're saying now is correct?

utterances.speaker: PERPARIM ISUFI
utterances.text: It's true that the police started to expel the populous and pointed them towards the train station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you wrote it differently, and I'm just drawing attention to that major discrepancy, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I've just had delivered copies of the document, which you may wish to have tendered as, was it 117A? But I do want to point one thing out, and that is that the document which has been disclosed to everybody, according to our duty, is as a result of a questionnaire taken in the camps. This particular one was taken on the 3rd of May, 1999. But it must be pointed out that these questionnaires are not signed by the witness or even acknowledged by them in terms of whether or not they're accurate. It's a questionnaire that people fill out, and the witness doesn't have an opportunity to see what's written. So on that basis, it's not truly a statement but it is a record of what someone says this witness once told them. On that basis, I would provide this to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have an exhibit for this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This one will be 117A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I agree. If this is the system that these exhibits are getting A and B, the way we've always done it is they're labelled sequentially. So perhaps over the adjournment we could go back, re-number the facts as Judge Kwon had it as it was the other day, and we'll re-number these ones so we'll come up to whatever the appropriate number is. Mr. Isufi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You're now free to go. We'll adjourn for half --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mr. Emin Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do I understand, sir, that you're 53 years old and that you are a Muslim of ethnic Albanian extraction? Is that correct? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand correctly that you're 53 years old?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And are you of ethnic -- Albanian ethnicity and that you live in Fushe Kosove?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you hold a Ph.D. degree from Pristina University. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In what field? What is your Ph.D. in?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the field of literature, Albanian literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I have three children; two sons and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, this place called Fushe Kosove --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could turn to Exhibit 83. Might the witness be shown that, and could we put it on the ELMO. Exhibit 83, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, you're being shown on the overhead projector that we call an ELMO an exhibit that is a map of Kosovo, a Kosovo atlas; and on page 6, there appears to be, about a third of the way on the bottom right-hand side, a community with the name of Fushe Kosove. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if we turn the page to number 7 - that appears to be the adjoining page - you see Pristina on page 7?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How far is your community, Fushe Kosove, from Pristina, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It is seven kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And what municipality is Fushe Kosove in?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Up until 1989, when we were deprived of the autonomy of Kosova, it was with Prishtina. As of that time, it is an independent municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, did you give a statement to the officers of the ICTY on the 24th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And subsequently, sir, were you shown a copy of that statement translated into your language, Albanian, and did you have a chance to read that on the 31st of January of this year, 2002?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes. They gave it to me and I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you at that time solemnly declare that the contents of that statement, as you then read it, were true and accurate to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I solemnly declare that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder whether that statement might now be marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I propose -- you have the full statement as 120. I propose to read a very brief outline of what is contained in that statement. Your Honours, according to my summary of that statement, it appears that on the 25th of March, 1999, there was a lot of movement of Serb police and armed civilians in the street near the witness's house in Fushe Kosove. That evening, a bomb was thrown in his house and there was a volley of automatic gunfire. The witness took other occupants of the house to a neighbour's house for safety. The following day, the witness returned to his home and found that the windows were broken and the house had been ransacked. His brother found 162 bullet cartridges around his home. The witness was also told at that time that 44 people were killed in the neighbourhood that night and was informed by a neighbour that the police were looking to kill the witness. Shortly thereafter, that neighbour, along with his wife and son, were killed. Well, the witness and some of his family fled to Pristina, where they stayed for three days, until the arrival of the Serb army and special police, who broke down the front door. He then describes that the army wore dark blue camouflage uniforms with VJ insignia and the Special Police wore lighter blue camouflage uniforms and masks. Both army and police were armed with automatic rifles. They separated the men from the women and children, threatened them at gunpoint and demanded money. The women had their identity cards taken from them and destroyed. The group were then taken to another neighbourhood, where they sought shelter at an Albanian-owned house. The following day, Serb police came to that home and told them to leave, saying, "Get out. You asked for NATO. Go to Macedonia or Albanian. Anyone who does not leave, we will catch and burn. This is Serbia." As they were leaving, the police told him, i.e., the witness, "Get out of here. Go to Albania." He then describes in his statement they were eventually directed by Serb police through Pristina in a convoy. A tank caused the column to divide into two, and the witness's group were directed to the railway station. En route, the column was stopped at a Serb checkpoint. The police had a list of names, and the witness saw that the list contained his name along with some other people known to him. The witness then gave the police a false identity. He was again asked for money and was told that if he didn't leave for Albania immediately, he would be killed. Snipers prevented members of the convoy from deviating from the route. The witness arrived at the railway station, from where he could see houses burning and homes being shelled. The witness waited at the railway station for the rest of his family for some three days, during which time he saw people being forced like cattle onto the trains by armed police. He describes that the trains so crowded that some died in the crush. He counted an average of 5 to 12 trains leaving daily, most at night. The witness finally got onto a train to Elez Han and was ordered to walk between the rails to the Macedonian border. He stayed there for six days and nights, awaiting his family to arrive, and noted trains and buses arriving every day with more people. He then explains details of how he did not want to leave Kosovo but was forced to do so by the Serb army and police. That's a very brief capsulated summary of what is contained in the witness statement that has been marked as an exhibit in these proceedings. Those are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which year did you get your doctorate from the university?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In 1989, 23rd of March, when Kosova's autonomy was stripped of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You got a doctorate at the department for the Albanian language and literature?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the branch of Albanian literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work after that, after you got your doctorate?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I worked in Drenovc, in the Institute of -- in the Ferronikel plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked there? I assume that you worked there even before you got your doctorate; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: From 1974, I was prevented to work in the education sector, and that is where I worked for the last ten years, until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why could you not work in the education field in 1974, or from 1974? Was this interpreted properly?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In 1964, I was a primary school student. In 1974, I was imprisoned in the high school [as interpreted] because I explained Albanian literature to my high school students.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How old were you in 1974? I can't get the math right.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was 24, 25 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do we understand each other? Are you speaking of 1974?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I'm speaking of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were you then? In school? You say you were in school, you were 24 years old?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. At that age, I was a graduated professor of literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were imprisoned because you worked in a secondary school. I assume that these were your pupils and you spoke to them about the Albanian literature and that's why they imprisoned you. Did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I talked to the children about the authors and works that were forbidden by the regime of that time, the communist regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But all the time, in the school programme, there was Albanian language and literature, and also at the university where you obtained your doctorate, there was a department for the Albanian language and literature. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were Albanian school pupils and definitely had to learn something about Albanian literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not controversial, but who are these authors whose works were forbidden, Albanian authors whose works were forbidden and you were arrested on account of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the indictment of 1974, it was said that I explained to the school pupils about Gjergj Fishta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who banned this? Who banned the mention of Albanian authors to pupils?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The authorities of the regime of that time, the administration at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in Pristina, where you worked, or in the province of Kosovo Metohija in general, were there Albanians in all high positions? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The Albanians in high position? There were even Albanians in high positions in the Federation at that time, not only in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was Albanians who arrested you because you spoke about that author who you mentioned just now, Fishta, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I was arrested by -- because of the communist mentality that prevailed at that time and infiltrated into the culture and literature of the people, and which replaced national culture at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was different: Were you arrested by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. I was arrested by the employees of a regime that replaced national ideology with communist ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... understand. These employees of the regime that you mentioned, were they Albanians or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were both Albanians and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you stand trial on any particular counts at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: After six months of investigation, I was released, but without the right to work any more in education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were in prison for six months and that you were then released, without standing trial?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not only in prison, but under very terrible kinds of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was in charge of this investigation? Who conducted it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It was led by the employees of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they Albanians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: They were both Albanians and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many of them carried out this investigation through interviews with you in 1974, during those six months?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: More than four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, because I didn't pay particular care to remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that they investigated you for six months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are dealing now with events a quarter of a century ago. It does not seem to assist this Tribunal to have evidence in such detail about events so long ago. They are nothing to do with the witness's evidence or his statement, which has to do with events, and serious events, in 1999. So will you move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it does have something to do with this, because he talks about measures of repression that were allegedly carried out against him, and also, at that time, practically all high positions in Kosovo and Metohija were held by Albanians, and in Pristina. But I shall move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you do not mention with a single word any consequence of the NATO aggression, or rather, the bombing; you just mentioned the date when it started, the 24th of March. Can you say why?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In my statement, I talked about the most important -- the most terrible genocide that was visited upon a people, when an entire geographic area was emptied of its population and the population was expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The statement refers to the NATO bombing. This is page 6. "Did not affect residential areas. I saw the bombing of Pristina airport." Is that right, Dr. Kabashi? "I saw the bombing of the barracks outside Pristina and I saw the bombing of the courthouse and the main police station."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The central Prishtina prison. That's right, Your Honour. It's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that during the bombing, which lasted for 78 days, 40 per cent of the bombs were precisely thrown on Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a matter for the witness. He deals with events which he himself saw, as far as the bombing is concerned, but fairly shortly after that, he left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Up until the day you left Kosovo. Do you claim that nothing in Pristina, or, as far as you know, in Kosovo and Metohija, was bombed, apart from those administrative buildings which you mentioned, including the barracks, the courthouse, the building of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about things that were bombed, only those things which I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From your statement, I understand that you are not a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, you haven't understood it. I was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And since when were you a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: From the day when you held a speech in Fushe Kosove, and under the -- 1997, on 28th of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were a member of the KLA. You meant 1987, did you, or was it not properly interpreted?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: On the 28th of November, 1997, when a teacher was killed in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. A moment ago you said you were a member of the KLA since I held a speech in Kosovo Polje [sic], and that was in 1987. Was the interpretation of that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I said because of the -- the reason was your speech in Kosovo Polje. From then, I saw that the only way for our people to win their freedom was by means of the gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I'm able to understand, it was then that you joined the KLA, that is to say, in 1997. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did you work in the interests of that movement from 1987 to 1997? How did you do that work in that period?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Everything that I could within my intellectual and human capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What, for example?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I prepared a lot of literature, I read a lot, I read my history, and then I explained to people and I worked out for myself that freedom cannot be taken for granted; it has to be won. And I supported every movement that emerged in Kosova after 1968, when I was imprisoned for the first time, down to 1989, when I was imprisoned for the last time. And all this enabled me to understand, and I made every effort to explain this to others, that only the path of war can bring us freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So since 1967 up until 1989, on several occasions, you were put in prison. We heard about one case at the beginning, but let me ask you how many times you were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not 1967, but 1968. I was imprisoned in 1968, when Albanian students demonstrated in Prishtina and the streets of Prishtina were covered with blood. At that time, I was in the third grade of high school. I have been imprisoned three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1974, you said. So in 1968 was the first time, and what about the third time? When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1981. That was after those major demonstrations in 1981. Was it in that connection?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was in connection with the demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that during the whole of that time, to which your explanations about your imprisonment relate, that during that whole period, the police structures and legal structures and structures of power and authority in Kosovo and Metohija were Albanian, or predominantly Albanian were the vast majority? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: If Your Honour will permit, I will answer -- I will reply to the accused, but this is not a matter to do with my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. When did you hear for the first time -- when did you hear for the first time of some terrorist actions perpetrated by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
