utterances.text: I'm not aware of the KLA having committed terrorist acts because it was not a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how would you call, for example, the planting of bombs in shops, marketplaces, bombs in public places, and the killing of civilians? Were those terrorist acts or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Civilians were not killed in operations of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, therefore, that in the actions of the KLA, civilians weren't victims, that they were not killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to get very far with this sort of argument. It will be for us to characterise these activities and to determine what happened. This witness can only really give evidence about what he actually knows himself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that, as you claim, from 1968 onwards, throughout all those years, and finally, from 1997, you were an active member of the KLA, the policemen that you mention, did they interrogate you unfoundedly with regard to your activities within the KLA, or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me. Either that, or the translation is not in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's not for the witness to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness explained and mentioned the names of two policemen who interviewed him with respect to the activities of the KLA in a way which was considered unfounded, and everything that he said gives rise and gives a basis for interrogation with respect to KLA activities. So I think the question is clear. As he was an active member of the KLA, why does he consider that he was not justly interrogated with respect to the activities of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It depends what the interrogation was. It's not going to help us to know what the interrogation was, but what you can ask him is what his activities were in the KLA. Can you help us with that, Dr. Kabashi? What did you do for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, I may respond to the accused's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't bother about the interrogation. The interrogation is irrelevant for these purposes. But can you help us as to what you did for the KLA? You say you were a member.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, definitely. I was responsible to help with finding accommodation for the displaced population from the zones where fighting was taking place. Then I was responsible to supply this population and the soldiers with footwear and clothes. Then I was also responsible to take care and to try and find the necessary food supplies for the displaced population and for the soldiers. Then, as far as I could and as far as I knew, I helped in the supply of the military hospitals, those that were and those that were being set up, to supply them with the necessary medicaments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the basis of everything that you have spoken about so far relating to your activities from 1968 onwards, are we able to conclude that you were a fighter of the -- an advocate of the anti-Serb policy?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was a fighter of the anti-Albanian policy, against anti-Albanian policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the relationships like in Kosovo Polje, where you lived up until 1998, all those years? What were the relationships like there? There were quite a lot of Serbs there, Albanians, and other ethnic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 4022 to 4033. groups too, and what were the relationships that prevailed in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Up until the day that the accused held his speech in Fushe Kosove, his notorious anti-Albanian speech, the relations in Fushe Kosove, as far as I know, were relations of an ideological brotherhood. As of that time, that is, 1989 onwards, these relations became those of open hostility because of the simple reason that Kosova plain, under the orders and dictate of the mechanisms of the power of the accused, had become the epicentre of the popular revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me any position that I made in what you called an anti-Albanian speech I made that was anti-Albanian? Can you tell me what it was that I said that could be characterised as anti-Albanian in 1989?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I am not obligated to remember by rote the speech of the accused, but if the Court is interested, I can find evidence to prove this in two places: In the archives of the Committee of the Communist League of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo then and the archives of the Central Committee of the then Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that that speech of mine was anti-Albanian and that it motivated you to undertake the actions that you explained to us. Now, if that is correct, if what you say is true, then you would have to know what it was in that speech that you thought was anti-Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he cannot now remember but refers us to a copy of the speech. We've had references to it before. No doubt in due course we'll get a copy of it. But for the moment, we can't go on over this ground again. Yes. Now, if you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You had occasion to see a copy of that speech here. Are you a member of any political organisation at present, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the reasons why, at the end of 1998 and 1999, the police patrolled part of the town you lived in?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Either you have not formulated the question properly or you -- you've mistaken the years. It's 1989 and 1999 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 1998 and 1999. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In addition to the reason that they wanted to show the muscle of the Serb forces, I didn't see any other reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about any kind of criminal activity for which the police patrolled the town at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't work in the investigation that is to know which criminal acts they have committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you didn't deal in any investigation. I assume that you went about your professional work, in addition to your KLA activities. Now, do you know, from that 1989 to 1999, how many of your colleagues and your fellow Albanians graduated and received doctorates at the department for Albanian -- for the Albanian language and literature at Pristina University?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: This is up to the administration staff of the faculty of Prishtina to know. If the Court is interested, I might ask them to give me documents. It is not relevant to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The fact is, we have heard evidence about this, and if you can help us, do; but if you can't, if you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not know -- I cannot give you any accurate figures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Albanian language and literature department at the Pristina University worked in the Albanian language right up until the year 1999, up until the war, actually? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fully aware of that, but it didn't work in the facilities of the university. But even this, I think, does not relate to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, then. Were you happy to see the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia take place?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I supported and approved the NATO actions because it was taking under protection a people that, on the basis of the plans of the Serb academy, was meant to be displaced and dismembered as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what plan on the part of the Serbian academy and sciences? You're talking about the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, are you not?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the programmes for the extermination of the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose programme? You said the Serbian academy's.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Of course I said the Serb academy. One of the programmes is titled "The extermination of the Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the Serbian Academy of Sciences?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which document of the Serbian academy speaks about the extermination of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: It is a document of 1884, until the one that you have implemented. One of Vladan Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a mistake? Did you say 1884, a document of 1884? That's what it says on the transcript and that's what the interpretation was. Did you actually mean 1884?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I mean the programme of Vladan Djordjevic, 1884, which has been described by world scientists as the book most full of hate against a people that has ever been written. But Your Honours, I think this is not relevant to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So did you strive for NATO aggression in your circle, or did you come out in favour of it publicly as well?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: The manifestation of my support for NATO was public. I didn't have any reasons to keep it secret, for the simple reason that on the day when I was -- when I left Fushe Kosove for Prishtina, I heard the alarm go off about the NATO airstrikes, which saved me from being captured by the Serb police and army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the start of the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, were there any conflicts between the KLA and the Ministry of the Interior and the army in the area that you're well acquainted with, that is to say, the Pristina area?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: In the Prishtina area, there were conflicts, but in Fushe Kosove area, there weren't any conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any urban -- whether there was any urban fighting in the Pristina area?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: During the NATO airstrikes, from the day I left Prishtina to take care of my family, I know nothing. For that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that somebody attacked your house on that particular day, the day you mention. Now, did I understand you correctly to say that that attack on your house was perpetrated by the police?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, by the police and by the local residents, who were drafted on orders as policemen and as army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were the attackers, the attackers on your house? Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I saw more than eight of them. Some of them I know personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they in a vehicle of any kind or were they in front of your house for you to be able to see them directly?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At the moment when they threw the bomb at my home, they got down off a vehicle which was often seen patrolling in front of the street, in front of the street before my house. The same vehicle -- they got into the same vehicle and left with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they opened fire on your house and then left; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. Before they threw the bomb at my home, then they shot at the window, thinking that I or someone else from my family will be standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they didn't enter the house?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, they didn't. They had not come to enter the house; they had come to kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you assume that then they would have entered the house, had they come to kill you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know that. You might as well ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle that you're talking about, was it an official vehicle? Did you see its licence plates? Did it have any kind of sign on it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: At that time in Fushe Kosove and Kosova, it didn't matter to us what kind of vehicles they were. Of importance it was that people in uniforms used to drive in them and patrol around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many policemen and soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia were killed or abducted in 1998 and 1999 by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No. This was not my field. I was not in charge of any sort of investigations in connection with this problem. This was something that the police dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know, since you were following what was going on, and I imagine that you were in the very focus of events, both in terms of your education and in terms of the position you held, do you know that only in 1998, over 1.800 attacks were carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says he doesn't know. Now, you should deal with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I will be dealing with his statement, his evidence too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Albanians were killed before the war started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not going to allow these questions. Just move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the name of Gashi Osmani?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I've never heard this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And have you heard of Enver Shala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a waste of time going through lists which the witness says he knows nothing of. This is the way in which your time is taken up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think that these are very important issues, very important questions. The witness himself has said that he held an important position within the KLA. There is an entire list of Albanians here that were killed by the KLA precisely in Pristina, where the witness had been working. The witness claims that he knew nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness about this, then: Do you know, in Pristina, dealing with Pristina, of any Albanians who were killed, as it is alleged, by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With some preliminary explanation, Your Honour, if I may explain. I didn't have any kind of function in the KLA. I merely did my duties as a citizen who is fighting for freedom. I don't know about these things and I was not involved in them, and I don't know how many Albanians were killed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said yourself that you're a member of the KLA. Do you consider yourself to be an accomplice, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is totally irrelevant. He said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about abductions of both Serbs and Albanians in 1998? Several hundreds of abductions. Do you know at least one?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: These are fabrications of Serbian propaganda which was spread all over the world as a pretext for the military and police operations in Kosova, and at this time the Albanians were fighting for freedom, and the accused had stimulated the KLA to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I led the KLA to kill Albanians in Kosovo; is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless you've got some particular questions to ask this witness about what he said in his statement, we'll bring this cross-examination to a close. It's no good debating these general political points. He said he doesn't know. Now, do you have any relevant questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me, all these questions are relevant, Mr. May. However, since you insist only upon that which is written in his statement:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that you went to the neighbouring house, together with your family, after these events.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That's right, with eight members of my family I went to a neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this neighbour a Serb or an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: He was an Albanian. There were no Serbs in my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went to the railway station with a column of other people. It is your assertion that the police had been looking for you, searching for you, and you avoided this only by saying that your name was different. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I went in this column of people to the railway station after the police had expelled me from my own house, from the house of a friend, and another house, that is, three times within the space of four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it was the police, according to what you have said, threw you out three times. That is one fact. The other fact is that the police had been searching for you - that is your assertion - and every time they threw you out, they could not find you. But they did throw you out. Is this logical, as far as you are concerned, this that you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I was thrown out twice by the police and once by the army, and the reasoning behind it is -- the reason why the police was looking for me and couldn't find me, that's up to the police to explain, but I'm explaining what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that, at the railway station, you waited for three days in order to meet your family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: That's right, for the simple reason that my family was very large and was scattered in three places in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you waited for three days at the railway station in order to get all of your family together. At the same time, it is your assertion that the police was making Albanians board the train and travel. How come nobody made you board a train during those three days at the railway station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: To be quite accurate, I waited three days and three nights at the railway station, and my turn came on the morning of the fourth day, when policemen forced me and members of my family into a goods train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in your statement you said that you waited for your family for three days at the railway station. You didn't say that you were waiting in a line at the railway station. You said that you spent those three days waiting for your family.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Prishtina was cleansed neighbourhood by neighbourhood and I was waiting for these neighbourhoods to be emptied. And members of my family were expelled two days after myself, and then we were left somewhere where I will call No Man's Land, on the border with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I wanted us to clarify another issue, actually, the question that I had put to you. You said two things in the statement: That you waited for your family for three days at the railway station, and a little while ago, you said that for three days you were waiting in a line in order to board a train. So my question is: Were you waiting for your family for three days or were you waiting in line to board the train for three days?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Even if I hadn't been waiting for my family, it was impossible to board the trains because of the crush of people who were being expelled by force from Prishtina. Moreover, I am of an age when it is hard to leave Kosova. And moreover, I was waiting in hope that I would be able to be joined by other members of my family, so that we could at least travel together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, what you've said just now, that there were so many people and you couldn't board the train, that you could have -- that had you been in a position to board the train on the first day, you would have done so rather than waited for your family?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never dealt in speculations of this kind. At this time, I wasn't interested in this kind of theorising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is no theory; these are two different statements. So were you waiting for your family or were you waiting in line to board the train?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't say theory. The interpreter translated the word "pandehma" as "theory," which I will say is suppositions, and at that time I was not dealing with suppositions. Even if I were not waiting for my family, I didn't have the chance to get onto the train, which was so crushed because of all these people who were being forced to leave Prishtina. I think I've made myself very clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it your assertion that the police was using force against people at the railway station in order to have them board the trains?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... using theory -- not only were they using violence, but -- but one -- if one of the citizens tried to go away and take some sidestreet, the police have killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any killings?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't see any killings, but I saw a dead person one day after, and I heard the shot, because I was only 200 metres away. And during all the time, the police encircled the station and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've had the hour which you are entitled to. Do you have any more questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not see a single killing personally?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I said I saw the police, I heard the shots, and I saw the person dead, dead persons, not only in the station, but also on the fourth day, early morning, when I boarded the train to leave Kosova from Prishtina to Fushe Kosove, I saw two dead corpses in the vicinity of the railway tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who had killed these people whose corpses were near the railway station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know. If I knew, I would have mentioned them by name and I would have taken them to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly if I say that throughout this time, in 1998 and 1999, you did not know about a single victim of the KLA at that time, or of the NATO bombing, as of the 24th of March onwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with these matters. We're not going over them again. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I would have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Kabashi, you said that in 1997, 1998, and 1999, as a member of the KLA, you worked on the displacement of persons, Albanians.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I mean the people who were displaced from the combat areas. Do I need to repeat this? Finding accommodation for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I have understood that. However, could you tell me: What is the number of persons in respect of these few years that you know about? What is the number of persons who were displaced, who moved to other places, to the best of your knowledge? Does that mean that they were moving away from the places where there were clashes between the KLA, on the one hand, and the army and the police, on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: There were many people in Prishtina. There were many other people in smaller towns. But at that time, in the first phase of the war, there were more people displaced from the Drenica area, and these people came to Prishtina and somebody had to look after them, and I was one of the people with this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was Drenica, all of Drenica, under KLA control for a while?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: For a time it was, but the larger part of the population were expelled beforehand by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about Drenica in relation to all of Kosovo and Metohija: How big is it? Which proportion of the territory does it encompass?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I can say Drenica, in relation to Kosova - and we won't use the word "Metohija" - is 27 per cent of the territory of Kosova. That's its geographical area. But it's a much smaller proportion of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, while you were in the KLA, that is to say, all the way up until the 25th of March, were you - how should I put this? - in civilian clothing? Did you carry out these duties in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there other persons in the KLA who wore civilian clothing and who carried out certain duties for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't have permission to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, not when you're in town; when you're out in the field, where there were skirmishes and when you were dealing with the displaced persons, that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: On trips, we did have weapons, but we dealt with these displaced people in the towns. We weren't dealing with them in the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to your statement, you said that a bomb was thrown at your house. You mentioned the damage incurred. Was anybody hurt, though?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Fortunately, nobody died. My elder brother was injured in the forehead and lost blood. But because there was no light at that time, we were stretched out on the floor, and this saved us from the blast. And I had also taken away my children beforehand, one day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the next night you spent in a cellar, 50 of you in a cellar three by three. That's what it says here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: We didn't spend the next night but that night, because the bomb was thrown at 9.45. On the same night, not myself but the remainder of the family, and the inhabitants of the neighbourhood - there were over 50 people, and they took shelter in a cellar which was three by three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of these people injured or hurt?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, with the exception of my brother, the others were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me about that night that you spent in the cellar. Did it have anything to do with the bombing that started on the previous day, the NATO bombing? Did that have anything to do with you being in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: We didn't go to the cellar because of the NATO bombing, but because my family, in the neighbourhood where we lived, were subjected to that bomb I told you, and the shot at my window. During the NATO bombing, we didn't go to any shelters. In fact, we didn't have any shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly like to draw your attention to page 4, paragraph 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you said that you had reached Vranjica [phoen], that you spent some time in a place called Vranjevac [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: When I left my home in Fushe Kosove, I spent the first three nights in the neighbourhood which was then called Dragodan, now Arberia, whereas the two other nights, I spent these nights in the Vranjevc neighbourhood which is now called Kodra e Trimave. These two neighbourhoods are adjacent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. But here you said on that day, that's when you were in Vranjica [phoen], and that night, there was fighting. Who was fighting during that night in Vranjevac [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I can't tell you for sure, but as far as I know from the media, you had here a witness who testified that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't tell us about what any other witness said. If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who fought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there was fighting, it had to be taking place between someone, because in the very next sentence, you say: "Four persons were killed and I knew two out of them." Did these persons have anything to do with this fighting that was taking place between someone? Who was fighting? Because you said that there was great panic, that there were a lot of gunshots and explosions. Again you're talking about fighting. "Where there was fighting," you say. And you also say that four persons were killed. So can you say who was fighting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He just answered that. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, let's try and finish this witness, if we can, before this adjournment. He says he doesn't know who was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. I need only two more minutes. As an amicus curiae, I'm satisfied with this answer, but please, let us now move on to page 6, paragraph 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, in response to the questions put by the Honourable Trial Chamber, you said that you had seen and heard the bombs that had fallen -- you said what you said, right. How far away is Dragodan? How far away is it from the place where the bombs were falling? If my understanding was correct, it was seven kilometres away. Dragodan is seven kilometres away from Pristina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Not from Prishtina; from Fushe Kosove. If you mean the night of the bombing of the State Security of Serbia building in Prishtina, the distance from where I saw -- witnessed the event, as the crow flies, is not more than 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Time is very important, so let me cut things short. Mr. Kabashi, all right. However, you did say that from Dragodan, you saw the bombing of the court! House. How far away is Dragodan from the courthouse?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I explained it. As the crow flies, from the place where I was sitting, it is some 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. And then you finally say: "In the neighbourhood of Dragodan, the blast broke windows." Is that correct, the way you had put it here, that the blast broke windows in the neighbourhood of Dragodan and that you realised that from the house where you were?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know about other houses, but in the house I was in, the windows of the third floor were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the explosion?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this of any significance in terms of your decision to leave Kosovo as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: EMIN KABASHI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had nothing to do with that. We were evicted by the army from Dragodan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing arising. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Kabashi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I felt it my moral obligation to come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, perhaps you can give us a list of the witnesses for whom Rule 92 bis submissions have to be made. As far as I can see, on your list of the 29th of April, it is every witness after number 3, including 3; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Well, 3, as I say, we found we have a difficulty with the 92 bis'ing process, so number 4 would be our next witness that we would propose to call this afternoon. 9 will not be a 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And -- yes, the rest of them, up to 18. So 3 to 18 but for 9, I believe, are the ones that we require rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So you formally make an application, then, for a ruling on those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I do formally make such an application. I'm just advised that number 16 may not be coming. We've just found out that 16 is not available. So that's one for which I will withdraw the application at this point. We anticipate that, up until Friday, number 9 will be testifying on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Hopefully that assists Your Honour's inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter over the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In response to this request, Your Honours, the amici have no observation, if that might assist the Court. We have no problem with the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now. 2.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon or Mr. Ryneveld, whoever is going to deal with this: We're looking at the witnesses 10 through to 18 on the list of the 29th of April, and also 4 to 8. There is one witness for whom we simply don't appear to have a statement, and that is number 13. Do you have 13 on the list? It seems, as far as we can see, to cover a totally different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Number 13 is likely -- excuse me just one moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The reason you do not have number 13 is that the process of 92 bis'ing, if I can use that word, has not yet been accomplished, so we can't submit the statement to the Court in its final form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the other statements, you have submitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, along with a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to say about this? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, I haven't got the statement of that witness, and I should have. I've asked your secretary -- I asked them this morning, and as far as I was able to understand, I will be provided with one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to make a ruling on that one, but as far as the others are concerned, on the list of the 29th of April, numbers 4 to 8, 10 to 12, 14, 15, 17, and 18 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution will call Mr. Gani Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be an announcement from the registry about the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. There's one clarification that we need to make. The originally-marked Exhibit 116.1 will now be 117 ter, and the previous exhibit marked 117 will now be marked 118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Gani Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Haradinaj, were you born on the 25th of May, 1956?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Stanovc i Eperm, in the municipality of Vushtrri, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 28th and 29th of May, 1999, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 2001, did you provide an additional statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 3rd of February of this year, 2002, in the city of Pristina, Kosovo, were you provided with a copy of the statements that you made in May of 1999 and October of 2001, and any relevant attachments, in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registry of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, I was provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that occasion, did you confirm that the copies of the statements that were provided to you were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would offer those statements into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Gani Haradinaj is married and has four children. He has lived in the village of Stanovc i Eperm in Vushtrri municipality, in Kosovo, all of his life, and he works at the thermoelectric power station in Obilic as a section manager. In his statements, Mr. Haradinaj describes how in early April 1999, he, his family, and other villagers left their village after Serb forces shelled the village and began to move through it. Mr. Haradinaj tells how he and his family then moved from village to village, from Breznica, to Dumnica e Eperme, to Ceceli, and finally to Studime e Eperme, seeking shelter and protection from advancing Serb forces. Mr. Haradinaj describes the formation of a convoy of thousands of civilians in the village of Studime e Eperme, which started to move in the direction of the town of Vushtrri in early May 1999. The witness describes how this convoy was attacked by Serb forces firing machine-guns and grenades, resulting in the deaths of dozens of civilians. Afterwards, the convoy was directed by Serb forces to the Vushtrri Agricultural Cooperative Farm, where the men were eventually separated from the women and children. The men, including Mr. Haradinaj, were taken to Smrekovnice Prison. Mr. Haradinaj describes the inhumane conditions there and how he was beaten, interrogated, and forced to sign a document saying that from 1998 until the 3rd of May, 1999, he had participated in terrorist acts. Mr. Haradinaj describes how, on the 23rd of May, 1999, he was taken with other prisoners by bus to the village of Zur, several kilometres from the border of Albania, and then forced to run to the border and cross into Albania. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My microphone wasn't switched on. Is it true with the Serbs from the village of Velika Reka and Grace, which are located one kilometre to the east and west of your own village, that you lived peacefully with them, without any conflicts, right up until the spring of 1999? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes. We each minded his own affairs. We didn't have any cooperation per se, but neither did we have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the problems began at the same time that the war began?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: The problems began earlier. They weren't so acute, I would say. With the beginning of the NATO airstrike, the Serbs started their problems to inflict the conflicts [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So with the start of the bombing, the Serbs started with problems. Now, do you consider the bombing also to be a problem?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: No, not at all. Bombing was something we were looking forward to because we considered it the only salvation for the Albania people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a technician, you were employed in the -- in Obilic as section manager, and you worked right up until the 24th of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I said was: You worked as a technician in the thermoelectric powerplant at Obilic, as section manager, and that you worked there right up until the 24th of March, 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I worked as a shift manager and not as a technician -- as a supervisor, actually. The fact is that I worked there until the NATO airstrikes began, and I went home. Then I had to join my family. I didn't find my family. My family was driven away by the Serb forces, who threw grenades at my house and at the entire village, and the entire population was obliged to flee from there in the direction of Breznice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as I understand it, the answer to my question is that you worked, but you were shift leader, up until the 24th of March, that is to say, until the war began. You occupied your work post at the thermoelectric power station of Obilic. While you were at your work post, did you have any problems because you were an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, we did. All the Albanians who were in key positions were dismissed from those positions and replaced by the Serbs. I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanians worked in the Obilic thermoelectric power plant?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure. It's not in my power to do that. But I know that Albanians were made to work only in the most difficult positions, and the responsible ones were given to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us roughly how many Albanians were employed in the Obilic power station.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the total number of employed workers in the company you worked for? I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I was not working in the administration; I was working in the production units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you're saying is you don't know how many people were employed in your company; is that it?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I think I was clear in my reply. It's not in my power to give you the figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haradinaj --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I don't even know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haradinaj, how long did you work with the company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked there from 1975 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me that you really ought to have even a rough idea as to the number of employees in the company. Can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would willingly wish to help you, but, frankly speaking, I don't know because it was not part of my duties. I apologise for not giving you an exact figure. I don't want to testify to something which I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't want an exact figure; just a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my sector, we were roughly 32 or 33. We were dealing with the chemical composition of the water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-three. Were they all Albanians?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: No, they were not all Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many of them would you say were? Half, two-thirds? Roughly, at least in your sector. Give us a rough estimate. It was a small sector, numbering 33, roughly.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There were two Romas and six Serbs. The others were all Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that with the start of the NATO bombing, you left your post to see to your family. So you said a moment ago, in response to one of the questions asked, that when the bombing started, you left your work post to go and tend to your family, take care of your family. And straight after that, you said that you left because the Serbs had let go the managers, one of whom you were. Now, which is right: Did you leave your work post in order to take care of your family or did you leave your work post because the Serbs dismissed you?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I think your question was rather long. It will be kilometres long. Please make it shorter and ask it slowly, and one after another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us stop this fencing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. No. Let's try and get a short answer to this matter. When the bombing started, you left your post; is that right? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the bombing started, with grenades from Velika Reka, and the family went to the mountains, only then I left my post, but it was not because of the NATO airstrike, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Why was it that you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had to join my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nobody is criticising you at all. You must understand that. We just want to know what the facts were. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you left your work post because of your family and not because the Serbs had dismissed you; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know where this confusion comes in. Was there any question of your leaving your post because the Serbs had dismissed you, at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I left my post because, as I said, I wanted to join my family after the Serbs had shelled the village, shot at the houses, at other houses, and driven the population out of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, as you say, that the Serbs, in the first days of April, without any evident reason or intimation, started bombing your village? Yes or no. Just a short answer.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes; without any reason, they shelled the village first, then the infantry troops entered, they looted and raided. It was in the early days of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the beginning of April, you say that the Serb forces, for no reason at all, shelled the village. Now, if that was at the beginning of April, as you yourself say, why then did you have to leave your work post a week before, on the 24th of March, or let's say the next day, 25th of March, to take care of your family?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: In the first days of April, we went to the village of Breznice and when we -- we left Breznice and then it was impossible to leave children in the mountains, and so I left my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about the time, about the dates that follow one another. You say that you left your work post on the 24th of March, when the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where does it say that? I do not recollect him saying that. When did you -- Just let's ask the witness. When was it that you left your work? Just a moment. When was it that you left your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left my -- I left my work sometime round about 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that you left work on the 12th of April. That is to say that until the 12th of April, you worked at the Obilic hydroelectric power plant?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I worked at a thermoelectric plant, not a hydroelectric plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say hydro. I said "thermal." I mean, I said the electric plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a question. Until the 12th of April, you worked at the Obilic power station?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that a little while ago you said, in response to my question, that you left your work post when the bombing started on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect it. I think this is simply going to confuse the witness. Just let him tell his story.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely the way I am putting questions in relation to his story, and I'm trying to follow what he's been saying. You can look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So that we get it straight: You left your work on the 12th of February because your village had been attacked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, Your Honour. However, one explanation: Before I left my work, my family and children had gone further away. They had left the place where we lived. And later, there was no way I could get to work, because this goes in phases, because we moved from various places in various phases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, in the upper third, it says -- I asked you: "On the 12th of April, you were working at the Obilic power station?" And the answer is, "Yes." And now the answer is that he left work in February. So can we finally come to the date when you left your work?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: It doesn't say anywhere in my statement that I left my job in 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript. It's been translated as February. Yes. Were you working until the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you live in Gornja Stanovc [phoen] now as well?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, in Stanovc i Eperm [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For how long was your village shelled?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Several times, every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And during that, what you claimed happened, were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the population went into the woods?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: They all left, and only a few old people were left, and this old man, Shaban Manxhiqi [phoen], was taken away and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who took this old man away and killed him?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: No doubt the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that? Did you see the Serbs take him away?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: He was merely found dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of what are you saying, then, that the Serbs killed him?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I can say in full responsibility that the Albanians did not kill Albanians, but he was killed by your hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you have been claiming, that Albanians did not kill Albanians, you are saying that he was not killed by Albanians, or rather, that he was killed by Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: In that I didn't see it, I believe that this is the case, and indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this old man who was killed, were there any other casualties in your village?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: While fleeing from Breznice to Dumnice on the 26th, there were also five casualties then. One of them was Ibrahim Prronaj, 55 years old, and his son, aged 20, and another one aged 20 whose name I don't remember, and a pregnant woman and another girl. They were buried at Dumnice. I saw these casualties myself. They were killed by mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of which month were you fleeing? You said the 26th.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Of April. April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: April. And this mortar fire that killed them, where was it coming from? Who was firing?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: According to eyewitnesses, the mortar fire came from Lumi e Madh, the village formerly known as Velika Reka, and it was aimed directly at the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying according to what eyewitnesses said, but you didn't see it with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: We only saw the casualties. It is not possible to see where the fire came from because Dumnice and Velika Reka are three to four kilometres apart as the crow flies, but I saw fragments of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything precisely about these Obilic plants and the KLA attacks precisely by mortar? Are you aware of these events?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Would you put the question again? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of KLA attacks against Obilic, that is to say, the company that you worked for, and also the area beyond that?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There were no KLA attacks anywhere near my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about attacks from the neighbouring village that came from the KLA? Just say yes or no. I'm not asking you for descriptions.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I can't describe it without going into long details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Are you aware of KLA attacks coming from the nearby village, the villages in the neighbouring area?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: What area are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely the area where your village is and where your company is. I'm talking about the area you come from.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: My village and my workplace are ten kilometres apart from one another, and so I can't really provide the answer you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that area, ten kilometres long, between your village and the place where you worked, are you aware of any KLA attacks there?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: On the road that I travelled from Stanofc to the highway, through Shkabaj, formerly known as Orloviqi, to Obiliq, there were no confrontations between the KLA and your forces anywhere along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any clashes in that area between the KLA and our forces, as you had put it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There were no KLA forces in my village. There were no KLA forces in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew of any attacks in that area of yours, attacks that were launched by the KLA against our forces, and the other way around.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I didn't see any, but according to the press and the television, there were attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see them. You described the following: Like the other inhabitants of the village, you started leaving Gornja Stanofc [phoen] when you saw Serbs dressed in camouflage uniforms entering your village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, I said this, but I should explain that there was no KLA there, and the residents fled, and it was the Serbian forces that drove away the population and not the KLA. That's what it says in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand what you have been asserting. How many houses are there in your village?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: About 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many houses were damaged during the shelling that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: According to statistics, about 70 per cent of the houses in Stanofc were burnt and shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Breznica from your village?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Between the one end of Stanofc and the beginning of Breznice, there are about four to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from the end of your village to the beginning, there is four or five kilometres, and you say that, from Breznica, you were watching the Serbs looting or torching houses in Gornja Stanofc [phoen]; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I think it's written well in my statement, because you can see one from the other through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. With the use of binoculars, as you say, four or five kilometres away. It can certainly be established on a map how far this is, actually. But you say that you saw all of it from there? You saw the Serbs entering the houses, looting them, burning them, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes. They looted and then they set the houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe that, how the Serbs looted the houses?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Quite clearly. They came with trucks, and your army guarded them and civilians went in and took what they wanted, and then the houses were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was looting the houses: Civilians or the military?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: In that they were together, they did it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that from a five-kilometre distance, you saw civilians entering houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that. He said that through binoculars he saw it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that two days upon your arrival in Brenica [phoen] or Breznica - I can't get the pronunciation of the village right - that the shelling of that village started?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: This question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You left your village and went to which village?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: To the village of Breznice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was this village attacked?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Two days after we left Stanofc, we left again and then started going up the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did you go away after two days?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Because Breznice too started to be shelled, from the lower part of the village. The houses started to be set on fire. The same thing happened as in Stanofc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see these forces that were shelling Breznica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I didn't see the forces, but I saw -- I heard the mortars. I saw the shells dropping in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you claim, as far as I could see in your statement, that they shelled the village with hand-held mortars is that right, or hand-held launchers?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: The shells I saw came from the launchers, from the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Hand-held. Do you know at which distance targets can be engaged from a hand-held launcher?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know. Your army knows, you criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't abuse the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see the launchers firing, except that you saw the shells fired from them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I am not clear. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to rephrase it. Since you are a layman, since you are not knowledgeable in such matters, how come you know that they used hand-held launchers?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Because I can tell the shells coming from the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And near Breznica, near the village itself, at that time were there any members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: They were on the move, but they hadn't taken up any positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them in Breznica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Whom? Whom do you mean did I see?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Members of the KLA. You say that they were on the move but they hadn't taken up any positions. Did you see them on the move in Breznica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, were they fleeing together with you from Breznica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: No. They were only escorting the population and returned to their position in Dumnice or elsewhere where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is it from Dubnica to Breznica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly. You're describing the events. You went from Breznica to Dubnica. You just mentioned Dubnica. So it's probably nearby. So how far, roughly speaking, is it from Breznica to Dubnica?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Roughly three, four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three or four kilometres. And you say that around the village of Dubnica, you came across the defence lines of the KLA. That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you claim that it was around the village of Dubnica that you came across, as you say, you came across the defence lines of the KLA. Is that right or is it not?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: After we left Breznice village, we headed towards Dumnice, and then it was when the KLA protected us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you come across the defence lines of the KLA in Dubnica, as you claim?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There were forces of the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you have said, you saw the KLA moving in Breznica, and three kilometres further off, in Dubnica, as you say, were the defence positions, as you call them, of the KLA. That means that in that whole area, Breznica-Dubnica, was where the KLA moved around. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: It is a very long sentence. I don't know why your sentences are kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, don't argue with him. He has a point, Mr. Milosevic. The questions are too long. I think the question seems to be: Were the KLA in Breznica and Dubnica? And I think your answer is: Yes, there were KLA there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, can we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Gornja Dubnica on that day, how many members of the KLA were there there?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember whether the members of the KLA were fleeing, or were they opening fire on the members of our forces?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: There wasn't any clashes among the KLA and your forces. Only the Serb forces fired at the people, at the civilian population, with mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The KLA was just fleeing; it wasn't doing any firing. Right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I think I was clear. There wasn't any confrontations between the KLA and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the KLA doing? You saw them on the move in Breznica, you came across their lines in Dubnica, three kilometres later. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: You draw such a complicated picture of the situation that I can't tell. I told you: The KLA was positioned in Dumnice village, and they just kept a vigil on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're claiming that the KLA, from those positions, didn't do any firing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any shelling of Gornja Dubnica, Upper Dubnica? Where the KLA positions were, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: From where, and which forces do you think did the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that in Dubnica there were KLA units present. Now, did our forces attack those positions of theirs?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: They did not attack the KLA positions; they attacked the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then the KLA had its positions in Dubnica. That's where the population was too, the inhabitants. The army or the police or the army and the police did not attack the KLA but they attacked the inhabitants; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, they attacked only the population, because they didn't dare attack the KLA. But they fired at the defenceless population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they avoided shooting at the KLA, did they?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Not they avoided it; their purpose was to inflict damage more on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And where were the civilians rallied in Dubnica? Where did they gather? At what place?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle of the village or in houses where they could find shelter, or on top of the tractors. When the Serb forces saw them, then they started to fire with mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the forces attacked the civilians, as you claim, where were the KLA positions at that time? Where was the KLA at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: The Serb forces were on a lower position, the KLA in the middle, the population on a higher ground, and the Serb forces used mortars against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have I understood this correctly: The KLA was in between the civilians and our own forces? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come, then, if they were in between the civilians and our forces, that they did not protect the civilians?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: It is easy to guess, because it is known what machinery you had and what weapons the KLA had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that in the valley, there were our forces, and then next came the KLA, and behind the KLA were the civilians; and our forces weren't shooting at the KLA, they were shooting at the civilians, skipping over the KLA. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I'm saying. But I can explain. There wasn't any close-range fighting. They shelled only from a distance, with mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But not at the KLA, but the civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the ones you mentioned, Ibrahim, Afrim, and Beslim, and the others, were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: Can you mention the names again, because they came very fast. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim, Afrim, Beslim.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I can swear on my heart that they were not members of the KLA, but they were in the convoy with me. Ibrahim was 65 years old. Ibrahim Prronaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Prronaj, yes. And how far is the village of Gornja Dubnica from Cecilija?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: It's a distance. I don't know exactly how far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Not to lose time establishing the approximate distance: Is it true that the KLA headquarters were in that village? Yes or no. Just say yes or no, and we can cut down on the time.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're asking about the base of the KLA in Ceceli or in Dumnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about Cecelija. Is that where the KLA had its headquarters? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: The KLA had its headquarters at Ceceli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but I know that he was a head teacher at a school beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many KLA members were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: Gani Haradinaj
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure.
